content: The document titled Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission of Hepatitis B Virus: Guidelines on Antiviral Prophylaxis in Pregnancy provides a comprehensive framework for addressing the global control of hepatitis B virus (HBV) transmission, particularly focusing on reducing the prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in children. The guidelines emphasize the importance of antiviral prophylaxis during pregnancy to prevent perinatal transmission of HBV. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that in 2015, approximately 257 million people globally were living with chronic HBV infection. The burden of HBV is particularly high in regions with low coverage of timely birth doses of the hepatitis B vaccine (HepB-TBD), such as Africa, where the 2017 coverage was only 10%. WHO recognizes HBV-related diseases, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), as significant global public health challenges and strongly recommends the inclusion of the hepatitis B vaccine in national immunization programs. A comprehensive approach to eliminating HBV transmission must address infections acquired perinatally, during childhood, and later in life. WHO has issued position papers on hepatitis B vaccination, updated in 2004, 2009, and 2017, recommending that all countries integrate HepB into routine immunization schedules and improve vaccination coverage for all children. The first dose of the vaccine should be administered as soon as possible after birth, ideally within 24 hours. As of 2018, 189 countries had introduced HepB for infants nationwide, with an estimated global coverage of 84% for the three-dose series. The global health sector strategy (GHSS) on viral hepatitis aims to eliminate hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, defined by a 90% reduction in incidence and a 65% reduction in mortality. For HBV, this translates to achieving less than 1% prevalence of chronic HBV infection in children under five years of age by 2020. This goal may require additional interventions, including the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HBV. PMTCT strategies involve testing pregnant women for HBsAg and implementing interventions such as administering hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) and peripartum antiviral prophylaxis. The GHSS also proposed a harmonized global target of less than 1% HBsAg prevalence in children under five years of age. Verification of a country's achievement of this target involves assessing the prevalence of HBsAg among children through serological surveys and evaluating immunization coverage. WHO has published technical guidelines to support countries in conducting nationally representative serological surveys to measure the impact of hepatitis B immunization programs. Regional mechanisms have been established to verify progress toward HBV control targets. For example, the WHO Western Pacific Region was the first to set a hepatitis B control goal, initially targeting less than 2% HBsAg prevalence among children aged five years by 2012, later revised to less than 1% by 2017. Independent expert panels assess whether countries meet these targets based on biomarker surveys and vaccination coverage data. As of 2019, 21 of 36 countries in the Western Pacific Region had been verified as achieving the regional target. Other regions have also established verification mechanisms. The South-East Asia Region formed an Expert Panel for Verification of Hepatitis B Control in 2018, and four countries have been verified as meeting the regional target. The European Region convened its first regional consultation on viral hepatitis in 2019 to discuss strategies and share tools for addressing common challenges. The Eastern Mediterranean Region was in the process of establishing an expert panel in 2019, while the African Region had not yet developed a verification mechanism. The document outlines criteria for verification, including evidence of low prevalence of chronic HBV infection among vaccinated cohorts of children and proof of high and sustained HepB immunization coverage. Nationally representative data from children born after the implementation of universal hepatitis B infant immunization are essential for verification. Additionally, coverage of timely birth doses of the vaccine (HepB-TBD) is a critical indicator. The guidelines emphasize the importance of harmonizing verification frameworks across regions to achieve the global target of less than 1% HBsAg prevalence in children under five years of age. Tools and procedures to support the verification process are annexed to the document, providing a standardized approach for countries and regions to assess progress toward HBV control.
